newsitem.title: UK: Healthy Yeltsin cheers investors in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Healthy Yeltsin cheers investors in Russia.

text.p: A healthy-looking Russian President Boris Yeltsin cheered up foreign investors on Thursday by promising to deal with just about all their major concerns about the way the country is run, analysts said.
"The over-arching point is that Yeltsin is back. He is reasonably strong and is in control," Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel McGovern said following Yeltsin's state of the nation speech.
In his 25-minute speech, the 66-year-old president pledged a range of economic and social reforms, including such key issues as tax collection and settling wage and pension arrears.
"All the points he made were what we hoped for...Across the board Yeltsin is pushing the right buttons," McGovern said.
The response on the markets was positive with prices rising for both locally and foreign traded dollar-denominated debt.
Old Soviet foreign commercial debt, which Moscow is close to restructuring with creditor banks, jumped more than one cent to just over 81 cents in the dollar following Yeltsin's speech.
Quite apart from the relief that Yeltsin, after months of illness, looked robust, analysts were also gratified by his intention to shake up the government.

"(The) potential for Yeltsin to see political advantage in realigning with proponents of radical reform, as public resentment mounts over growing income inequality and chronic wage and pension arrears, creates a genuine opportunity for investors in Russian debt," Paribas analysts, Stuart Brown, said.
Reformists in the cabinet should greatly increase the chances for growth and a better fiscal performance, he added.
There has been concern among investors that the reform process was beginning to lose its impetus, though they will now want to see the promises put into action.

"But he's gone straight to the problems which face Russia. With Yeltsin adding his weight and being prepared to reshuffle the government, one can now be somewhat reassured," Chase analyst Robin Hubbard said.
Many analysts are hoping that in the reshuffle, expected within days, Yeltsin will put his current chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, at the head of his economic team.
"If Chubais is picked it will be an unequivocal plus for Wesern investors," McGovern said.

Chubais is a strong advocate of market reform and would certainly give compfort to the International Monetary Fund which is currently looking at fresh funding for Russia, he added.-- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7770 (fax +44 171 583 7239)
